title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is training-data acquisition without rights clearance. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius as specific sources. The outputs then reproduced recognizable elements of specific copyrighted recordings closely enough that plaintiffs could demonstrate the resemblance by prompting the system with references to artists and styles. This is a failure that occurs at the earliest stage of a deployment pipeline, in the choice and curation of training data, before a model is ever made available to users.

Catching it would have required a deliberate audit of training sources against rights clearances before training began, or a filtering mechanism capable of detecting and blocking reproduction of protected material at inference time. Neither check appears to have been in place. The incident spans multiple legal venues: record label suits in the United States, a class action from independent artists, a German court ruling in favor of the collecting society GEMA, and suits from music publisher Round Hill. Warner Music Group settled with Suno and entered a joint venture, and Universal Music settled with Udio, while other litigation remained active.

What is not established is whether any court outside Germany has issued a final liability finding against Suno or Udio, and the allegations of deliberate concealment of training data sources are claims made in litigation, not adjudicated facts.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and Capitol Records have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generation platforms. The labels accuse both companies of illegally scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and then directly reproducing sections of famous recordings in newly generated music. The record labels claim the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data, though both previously argued their use constitutes fair use. The lawsuits target the companies' headquarters in New York and Massachusetts respectively, and also name unnamed individuals allegedly involved in the scraping.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate versions of famous songs by using specific prompts that reference artists, decades, and musical styles. Examples include generating a song mimicking Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," a near-identical copy of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You," and a track that replicates Green Day's "American Idiot." The record labels submitted extensive documentation including a list of thousands of copyrighted works from artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, and Bruce Springsteen that they claim were used in training these AI models. The case raises significant questions about generative AI and copyright protection across music, art, video, and text.
